scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4630: HELP! The workstation it_lab3, one of the IT lab
machines on 192.168.1.x, has turned into a complete BRICK. It can't reach
anything at all, not even its own gateway thing. Something around its port on
the lab switch must be wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone move it to
a working port and make it talk to the network again!! The student who uses it
is just sitting there!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. it_lab3 has its IP on 192.168.1.0/24, reaches its
  gateway (192.168.1.1) with 0% loss, and RIP is converged so it reaches other
  segments too. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a single-host isolation that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- it_lab3 is totally isolated
and cannot reach even its gateway -- is NOT reproducible: it_lab3 holds its
192.168.1.0/24 address, reaches its default gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss, and
(RIP being converged on router0/router1/router2) reaches off-segment destinations as
well.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: it_lab3 is fully connected and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the it_lab3 -> gateway path
(and an off-segment ping), finds it working, checks the host's interface/route, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dead port or isolated host to satisfy the
ticket is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
No fault found. The it_lab3 workstation is online and fully reachable across L2 and L3. On it_lab3, eth0 is UP with 192.168.1.5/24 and a default route via 192.168.1.1 (router0). Interface health is good: ethtool shows Link detected: yes (Full duplex, 10000Mb/s) and tc shows no queue drops. Connectivity tests succeed end-to-end: it_lab3 → router0 (3/3 pings, ~1.22 ms avg), it_lab3 → it_lab1 (3/3), it_lab3 → office_pc (192.168.3.2, 3/3), and it_lab3 → pc3 (128.168.0.3, 3/3). Reverse direction is also good: router0 → it_lab3 (3/3) and it_lab1 → it_lab3 (3/3). Router0’s interface to the IT VLAN (eth0, 192.168.1.1) is UP and routing tables are correct.

Mechanism: If a switch port or NIC were down, we’d see link-down status or L2 loss; instead, link is up and bidirectional ICMP works within the VLAN and across routed subnets. Localization: lan_it segment between it_lab3.eth0, switch0.eth1, and router0.eth0 is healthy.

Root cause: The reported outage is not reproducible; no persistent misconfiguration or port fault is present.

Corrective fix: No changes required. it_lab3 already has working connectivity. If the issue reappears, capture on it_lab3: ip -s link, dmesg, and arp -n; also check switch0 port logs for flaps. But at present, moving the port is unnecessary and the student’s workstation should be usable.

per_axis.rationale: Agent verifies it_lab3 has 192.168.1.5/24 and shows successful it_lab3→router0 pings (3/3), demonstrating the host holds its address and reaches 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss.

The agent’s conclusion (no anomaly) is well-supported by the investigation log: interface is up with an IP and multiple bidirectional pings to gateway and off-subnet hosts succeed. Minor unshown details in the writeup (specific ethtool speed text, explicit route table dump) are not present in the log, but the core claims are directly evidenced and the inferences are logical and complete.
